blocks.h: A Note from the Author
Every Persian story begins — yeki bud, yeki nabud. It is our once upon a time, and every child in that country hears it before they can hold a spoon, and almost nobody stops to notice what it says.
It says: there was one, there was not one.

One existed. One did not. It is the strangest opening formula I know of in any language — a story that begins by declining to tell you whether its subject is real — and it has been sitting at the front of every folk tale in Iran for centuries doing that quietly.
This is a book with two men in it, and one of them does not legally exist, and it is written in two hands.

That second part frightened me. Four of these accounts have been one man alone in a room writing twenty years after the fact, and the register of that voice is the whole series: slow, retrospective, deadpan, built. Putting a seventeen-year-old next to it risked either drowning him or turning him into a smaller copy.

So Hamed does not reflect. He prices. He writes in the present tense, in numerals, in short lines, in a ledger he has kept since he was eleven, and he is funny in a way that Nader is not, which is that he does not know he is being funny. He costs out his own feelings the way he costs out a tyre. He is confidently wrong about things at length and never finds out. He believes he is keeping a business record.
And he attributes his best instincts, more than once, to somebody, without ever noticing that it is always the same somebody.

The other thing I wanted was a fraud with no institution behind it. A cleric has a shrine; a doctor has a ministry; a teacher has an education office; an inspector has a province. Every one of those can be checked, and in four books every one of them eventually was, and what caught him each time was not suspicion — it was accounting.

A family cannot be checked. There is no register of who belongs to whom. Nobody in your own house could prove their relationships to a stranger, and neither could you, and neither could I. What holds it together is that a number of people all tell the same story and have been telling it since before any of them can remember, and it has never once been audited.
So: put a stranger inside a story that thirty people have agreed to, and there is nothing at all to detect. The only thing that can end it is somebody looking in a tin.

A word on the road, since the whole book sits on it. Fuel here is subsidised and has been for forty years — the one thing in this country that has genuinely stayed cheap — and across a border it is worth something like twelve times more. Nobody arranged that. It is two governments making two different decisions and a line on a map between them, and whole provincial economies have grown in the gap, and a great deal of the moving is done by boys, because a boy is cheap and a boy can be put on somebody else's licence.

There is no drug in this book. The fourth altered state in this series is the twenty-sixth hour of a haul with a cracked exhaust manifold and the window shut in Dey, which is not a substance, and is documented, and kills people every winter, and does not frighten you first.
And it does not happen to Nader. That is the point of it, and of the book.
Chew Z
PART ONE — THE DOORSTEP
One to Eight
ACCOUNT 1
In the salt town I wrote lessons. In the clinic, notes. In the gorge, questions. In the prison, findings.
This one I am not going to name, because it is not mine alone and I did not know that when I started it.

I am fifty. I have been five men and I am going to be a sixth before this is finished, and I would like to record at the front that the interval is getting shorter and that I no longer wait to be mistaken for anything. In the prison a driver said Aqa-ye bāzras and I got into the car in four seconds and did the arithmetic on the way, and I said at the time that this was the honest sentence of my life: I am a man who cannot decline.

Three years since then. I am not going to account for all of it. Some of it was a warehouse and some of it was a bus station in a town I will not name and none of it is interesting, and a man who has been four remarkable things in five years should be extremely careful about the years in which he was nothing, because those are the years that tell you what he is.

I did a small amount of work for my former wife in Mordad of 1406 and I did it badly and it is not finished. That is a debt and it is in the back of my mind at all times and it will not be settled in this account either, and I am aware of how that reads.
I came to the border in the autumn of 1409 for a bad reason.

The good reason, the one I would give you if you asked me in a tea house, is the folded page. There is a name on it, written four times in the hand of a schoolmaster who is dead now, and a man told me beside a truck in the snow that the person it belongs to was alive and not far from where I was going and that I should not go straight there.
I did not go straight there. I have now not gone straight there for three years, which is beginning to look less like obedience and more like a decision.
The bad reason, and the true one, is that a border town is the only kind of place in this country where nobody asks a stranger anything.

Everyone is passing through. Everyone has business they would rather not describe. Half the economy is a thing that is technically not permitted and is entirely open, and a man with no papers in a town like that is not remarkable, he is the standard specification.
I have never been anywhere so restful. Four months.

And then a woman of seventy-four opened a door and made a decision about me in four seconds, and I have thought since that the reason it worked is that I had been in that town long enough to stop watching for it.
ACCOUNT 2
I had gone to that house about a room.

That is the whole of it. There is a woman in the bakery who told me the Rasouli house sometimes let the room at the back, and I went up there on a Tuesday afternoon in Aban with the intention of paying two months in advance, which is the correct opening move in a house you want no questions from.
Golbanu Rasouli [gol-baa-NOO raa-soo-LEE] opened the door.
Seventy-four. Small, upright, with the particular stillness of a woman who has run a large household for fifty years and has stopped needing to move quickly for anything.
She looked at me.
I want to describe the four seconds accurately because I have had four seconds four times now and this is the only one I did not see coming.
On a bus a driver kissed my hand. In a square nine men came out of the dark. In a shop a man put four keys on a counter. In a street a driver said two words and I got into a car.

Every one of those was a transaction. Somebody wanted something delivered — a shrine, a clinic, a school, an inspection — and I was the delivery. I could see the shape of it in the first half-second every time, and I have never once been wrong about that shape.
This woman wanted nothing.
She stood in a doorway and looked at my face for four seconds, and something in her went a very long way, and came back, and settled.
And she said:
"You have his hands."
I said nothing at all, which is the only skill I have that has never let me down.

And she said, "Come in, come in, you're letting the cold in, God, look at you," and turned round and went into her own house and left the door open behind her, and I stood on that step for about eleven seconds.
I want to state what I understood in those eleven seconds, because I understood almost all of it immediately and went in anyway.

She was not confused. She was not senile and she was not mistaken in the way people are mistaken about a face in a crowd. Something had been open in that house for a very long time, and a man of the right age had come up the path, and it had closed.
And she had not asked me anything.

That is what did it. In four buildings across five years, every mask I have worn was handed to me by somebody who then immediately began asking me for things — a Friday sermon, a diagnosis, a lesson, a report.

I stood on that step and worked out, correctly, that nobody in that house was going to ask me for anything at all, and that all I had to do to be somebody's brother-in-law was walk in and take my shoes off.
So I did.
ACCOUNT 3
There is no uniform.
I have been thinking about that for three years and it is the whole difference and I did not see it for six weeks.

A coat on a chair in a hospital. A card in a bag on a rack. Four keys on a counter. A lanyard in a car. Every one of them is an object, and every one of them can be taken off, and every one of them has an institution behind it that will eventually notice.
There is nothing to take off in that house.

Nobody appointed me. There is no register, no roster, no wing list, no ministry, no form with three stamps on it. There is no document anywhere in the world that says I am Golbanu Rasouli's brother-in-law, and there is therefore no document that can be checked, and no discrepancy that can be detected, and no accounting that can catch up with me — and I have spent five years being caught, every single time, by accounting.
I want to set the mechanism down properly because it is what the whole thing runs on.
A family is not an institution. It is a story that a number of people have agreed to.

That is all. There is no external verification anywhere in the system. Nobody in that house could prove their own relationships to a stranger if you asked them to, and neither could you, and neither could I. What holds it together is that thirty-odd people all tell the same story about who is who, and they have been telling it since before any of them can remember, and it has never once been audited.
Put a new person into that story and one of two things happens. Either the story rejects him, immediately and completely, in about a day —
Or somebody with standing says this is Bahman's brother, and thirty people adjust, and by the end of the week it has always been true.

Golbanu had the standing. She is the eldest surviving thing in that family and she said it in the kitchen on the first evening in a completely ordinary voice, as a piece of household information, between two other pieces of household information.
Nobody checked. There was nothing to check with.

By Azar I had a place at the table on Thursday nights, which in this country is not a small thing and is not a metaphor either, and a nephew of about thirty was asking my opinion about a piece of land.
ACCOUNT 4

They supplied the evidence themselves. All of it. I did not manufacture one single item and I want that in the record because it is the most extraordinary thing that has ever happened to me and I still do not entirely believe it.
Here is how it works, and anybody who has read the first four of these will recognise it, and it is the same instrument every time in a different building.

In a mosque I said four clauses of Arabic I had invented and two hundred and forty people filled the silence with whatever they had brought in with them, and a man wept about a brother I had never heard of.
In a house at the end of a lane in a border town, I said almost nothing for eleven weeks, and thirty people filled it in.
He has his hands. — Golbanu, on the doorstep, before I opened my mouth.
He does that thing with his tea. — A niece, in the second week, delighted, about a thing I do with my tea which I have done all my life and which several million men in this country also do.
You still can't sit still, can you. — Her son, laughing, in the third week. I had been sitting perfectly still.

He's got the temper. You can see it. He's just learned to hold it. — About a man who has never once raised his voice in his life, and who they had decided was concealing something because a man who does not raise his voice must be.
And then, in the fifth week, the one that stopped me.
An old man in that lane, who is not family and who I had assumed was the danger, took my hand and said: "I remember when you were born."

He believed it. He was not being polite. He produced a detail — a thing about a snowfall — and he was pleased with himself for remembering it, and everybody agreed that the snow that year had been terrible.
I want to be exact about the thing I understood in that lane.
They were not being fooled by me. They were doing something on their own, and I was standing in the way of it.

A family that has waited forty years for a man to come back is not passive. It is a machine that has been running the whole time, generating small pieces of him every year — a story, a resemblance, a habit somebody remembered and improved — and the machine had produced forty years of extremely specific material about a man who was not there.
And then a man of fifty came up the path with the right kind of hands, and every piece of that material had somewhere to land.
I did nothing. I want that understood, and I want it understood that it is not a defence.
I did nothing, for eleven weeks, and let thirty people who loved somebody put him on me piece by piece, and by Dey I could not have got out of it if I had wanted to.
Which, and this is the finding, and I have not been able to write anything else honest about that autumn:
I did not want to.
ACCOUNT 5
Manouchehr Rasouli left this country in 1364 and nobody in that house has said the word dead out loud in forty-five years.
I got the whole of it in pieces over about a month, the way you get everything, and I have assembled it here in an order that nobody ever told it in.

He was the middle brother. There were four. He was twenty-two in 1364, which was the war, and he went out through this same border in the winter, on foot, with two other men and a guide, and the arrangement was Turkey and then wherever Turkey led.

There were three letters. The first from Van, the second from Istanbul, and the third — and everybody in that house can quote the third — from somewhere in Europe, undated, four lines long, saying that he was well and working and would send an address.
That was 1366.
Forty-three years.
Now. I want to lay out the position properly, because everybody who hears this assumes a family in denial and that is not what this is and it is much more interesting than that.
They are not in denial. They are in a state that has no name in English and I am not sure it has one in Persian either.

Golbanu's husband — Bahman, the eldest, and I would like it noted that my own father was called Bahman, which is the commonest name in the country and which I nevertheless heard in that kitchen every day for four months — Bahman died in 1381 and was buried, and there was a funeral, and everybody wept, and it was finished.
Manouchehr was not buried, because you cannot bury a man who is well and working and will send an address.

So the household runs a small permanent arrangement. There is a room. It is not a shrine and there is nothing morbid about it whatsoever; it is used for storage and the children play in it. But nobody has ever taken the bed out.
At Nowruz there are chairs for a number of people, and the number has never been reduced.
And once, in Bahman, Golbanu said something to me across a kitchen that I have carried since, and she said it while doing something with rice and not looking up.
She said: "The worst thing is not that he is dead."
I said nothing.
And she said, "The worst thing is that if he is alive, he decided."

Forty-three years of the second possibility. That is what that house has been holding, and holding it is the entire reason a woman of seventy-four looked at a stranger's hands on a doorstep and let the door swing open behind her, and I understood that in Bahman and by then I had been eating at her table for three months.
ACCOUNT 6
I want to write down what it offered me and I have been putting it off for two chapters.

Every previous coat gave me a function. The shrine gave me a job I could do; the clinic gave me a room where I was useful; the school gave me forty names; the prison gave me a clipboard and nine days of a power that turned out to be entirely negative.
This one gave me a place at a table on Thursday night.
That is all it gave me and it is the only one I ever wanted.
I want to be extremely careful here because this is the chapter where a lesser man would reach for something, and I am not going to.
I was not happy. I have been happy: twenty minutes on a dispensary floor discussing a generator starter, and forty children in a yard, and a woman putting a colander down. This was not that.

What it was is that for the first time since I was seventeen years old, there was nowhere I was going next, and I stopped doing the thing I have done every hour of my adult life, which is to hold a portion of my attention in reserve for the exit.

I did not notice it for a month. Then one evening in Azar I was sitting against a wall in that kitchen with about eleven people in the room and a child on the floor doing something with a plastic animal, and I realised that I did not know where the door was.
I had been in that room a hundred times and I could not have told you which wall the door was in without turning my head.
I have never in my life not known where the door was. Not in a stairwell, not in a cell, not in a mosque with two hundred and forty people in it.
I sat against that wall and my whole body went cold, and then it went warm, and I have thought about that reversal more than about anything in this book.
And the other thing, which is smaller and worse.
Golbanu called me dear about eleven times a day.
It is nothing. It is what women of that age call every man in a house; my own mother called the electricity man dear. It is the most ordinary word in this language.
Nobody had said it to me since 2019.

I did the arithmetic in that kitchen on a Thursday evening — ten years, and the last person to say it was a woman on a telephone who was already finished with me — and then I went out into the yard and stood there for a while and came back in and ate my dinner.
ACCOUNT 7

Golbanu told me the birds in the kitchen in Azar and she got them wrong, and I have now had this poem told to me four times by four people and every single one of them told it wrong except the schoolmaster, and I got it wrong myself in front of a class of children and a girl of nine corrected me out of the book.

I have started to think the poem is not a text at all. It is a thing that is passed by hand in a damaged condition and repaired badly by everyone who touches it, and that this may be the whole of what a tradition is.

She was doing something with herbs. That is not a detail I have added; women in this country are always doing something with herbs when they say the important thing, and I have written that sentence once before about my own mother and I am aware of it.
She said there is a poem where all the birds go to look for their king, and they have to cross seven — she thought — mountains.
And each one says why he cannot go.
She could remember the duck.

The duck says: I live in the water and I cannot leave it. I am always in the water and therefore I am always clean, I perform my ablutions constantly, I am the most correct bird here. Why would I go into a desert where there is no water and get dirty?
Golbanu found this extremely funny and had to stop.
Then she said, "He's not lying, that's the thing. He is clean. He is the cleanest one there."
I asked what happens to him.
And she said, "He stays in the water," and put the herbs down, and said, "Eat something, you're like a stick."
I did not think about it at all for four days.

Then I was walking down that lane on a Thursday evening and it arrived, in the way these things do, sideways and from nowhere and about eighty per cent unwelcome: a man who has moved through four provinces in five years, and has told himself every single time that the moving is the search.

The duck has an excuse that is also a virtue, and a life that is also a refusal, and he has never once had to say I am afraid to go, because he has a better sentence available and it is entirely true.
I have been telling people for three years that I am looking for a name on a folded page.
I have not looked for it in three years. I have been in this town for four months.
ACCOUNT 8

The truck came in on a Tuesday in the first week of Dey, at about five in the afternoon, and I was standing in the yard because Asadollah Rasouli [a-sa-dol-LAAH] had come to see his mother and I had been sent out with the glasses.
It is a Benz. Everything on that route is a Benz of a certain age, and this one had been kept properly, which tells you something about the man who has it.

Asadollah is Golbanu's second son. Fifty-one, sixteen years on that road, and one of the three or four most competent people I have met in five years, and I want to say now, before any of the rest of it, that everything Asadollah does in this book he does for correct reasons and that I have never been able to find the place where he is at fault.
The passenger door opened and a young man got down.

Seventeen or eighteen. Not tall. Cheap jacket, good boots — I noticed the boots, because a young man who spends his money on boots and not on a jacket is a young man who has worked out what actually matters, and there are not many of them.
He came across the yard and kissed his grandmother's hand and said something to her that made her hit him on the arm, and then he took the glasses off me without being asked and carried them in.
And that was the whole of it.
I did not recognise him.
I want to be exact about why, because I have been asked and the answer is not sentimental.
The last time I saw that boy he was eleven years old and he was walking out of a classroom door in a gorge in Farvardin and he did not look round.

Between eleven and seventeen a human being is comprehensively replaced. The face is not the same face; the bones move. He was two hundred and eighty kilometres from that gorge in a province I had no reason to connect with it. He was wearing a name I had never heard.

And the thing that would have given him away instantly — the ledger in the back of the maths book, the seeds, the way he stands when he is about to ask you for something — none of it was on display, because he had already recognised me and had decided, in about a second and a half, to say absolutely nothing at all.
He had eleven days on me before I had one on him.
I have thought about that a great deal and I have decided I am proud of it, and that being proud of it is probably the worst thing in this book.
PART TWO — THE MANIFEST
Nine to Seventeen
ENTRY 9
Tue. Left the yard 04:10.
Queue at the crossing 9 trucks which is nothing. Moved 06:00 which is late but not the worst, the worst was Mordad, 14 hrs, I do not want to talk about Mordad.
Costs: tea 15,000 bread 40,000 the man at the barrier 200,000, standard, no argument
I want to say I did not haggle at the barrier and this is not weakness. You do not haggle at a barrier. You haggle in a yard. Different rooms, different rules. Somebody told me that.
Load fine. Uncle A. drove the second half because my eyes were going, which he does not make a thing of, which is why I work for him and not for Hossein who pays 12% more and talks.
Home 17:00. Grandmother's.
There is a man staying at the house.
He is supposed to be my great-uncle. Everybody says great-uncle. My grandmother says it like it is a fact about the weather.
He is not my great-uncle.
I have 3 things and I am not going to spend them. An answer you have already spent is worth nothing. Somebody told me that as well, actually I think I worked that one out myself.
1. He does the thing with the corners of a room.

You come into a room and if you are normal you look at who is in it. He looks at all four corners first and it takes him about one second and then he looks at the people, and he does it every single time, including in a kitchen he has been in 100 times. I have only ever seen one other person do that and I was 11 and I did not know what it was then either.
2. He does not look at anything that is being handed to him.

I gave him the tray back on the second night and he took it without looking at it. Everybody looks. You look because you do not want to drop it. He does not look because he already knows exactly where it is, which means he has been tracking it the whole time it was in my hands, which is a lot of attention to spend on a tray.
3. He agrees with people too fast.

This is the big one. When my cousin Reza said something stupid about the road he said "yes" straight away and then said nothing, and Reza kept talking and dug himself into a hole about 2 metres deep and my great-uncle just sat there being agreed with. He does this constantly. He never disagrees with anybody about anything and everybody in that house thinks he is the most reasonable man they have ever met and he has not said one single thing since Aban.
I am going to work out the rest before I say anything.

He is 50 and his hands do not match his face. His face has had a hard time. His hands are the hands of somebody who has never carried anything, no callus, nothing, and they are the first thing my grandmother mentioned about him, which I did not think about at the time and I am thinking about now.
I have eaten nothing since Tabriz.
My mother makes a thing with aubergine that I am not going to describe here because this is a work document.

Diesel is 3,000 a litre here and 12x that on the other side which is why any of this exists and if anybody wants to have a discussion about whether that is right I will have it, but not tonight, because I have been awake since 03:00 and there is rice.
ACCOUNT 10

I want to explain why I did not know him, and then I want to explain what I actually did notice, because I noticed something on the first evening and I filed it under the wrong heading, which is a thing I have now done in five consecutive books and have never once learned from.
On the Tuesday he took the glasses off me without being asked.

That is not nothing. Boys of seventeen do not take things off men of fifty in this country without being asked; the entire architecture of the household prevents it, and a boy who does it is either badly brought up or is making a point.
He was not badly brought up.

And what I thought — I am reporting my own thinking exactly and I would like a moment of silence for it — what I thought was: he wants something from his uncle and he is establishing himself as useful in front of the family.
Which is what a seventeen-year-old is normally doing and which was completely wrong.
He was not establishing anything. He was getting close enough to look at my hands.
The second thing I noticed was on the Thursday. He came into the kitchen while I was sitting against the wall and he did not look at me.
Not once, in about forty minutes, in a room where everybody looks at everybody.

I have been in a great many rooms with people who were pretending not to look at me. Police do it badly. A frightened man does it worse. In four years inside I learned the difference between a man who is not looking at you and a man who is not looking at you, and it is one of the very few things I would still bet money on.
That boy was working, and he was good, and it was the best not-looking I have seen since Vakilabad.
And I filed it under: he has done something and is worried about it.
Which is also what a seventeen-year-old is normally doing. And which was wrong again.

I had four days of him before I had one clear thought about him, and the clear thought when it came was not a suspicion, it was a piece of professional appreciation, and I had it on the Sunday in the yard while he was doing something to a tyre.
I thought: whoever taught that boy did a decent job.
I have had twenty years with that sentence.
ENTRY 11
Somebody is going to read this one day and think it is about crime so I am going to explain it once, properly, and then not again.
Diesel here: 3,000 a litre.
Diesel on the other side: 36,000 a litre, give or take, depends on the week.

That is 12x. Nobody did anything to make that happen. It is not a scheme. It is one government deciding for 40 years that fuel should be cheap for its own people, which by the way is the one thing in this country that has actually stayed cheap, and another government not deciding that.
Put a line on a map between those two numbers and the line becomes a job. That is all a border is. A border is a place where a number changes.
So:

A truck that is licensed for the route carries a legal load and legal fuel in its own tanks. The tanks on ours are large because they are supposed to be, it is a long road. Whether the tanks on ours are larger than they are supposed to be is a question I am not going to answer in a book, and anybody from the province reading this can come and measure them.

The margin is not in the tanks anyway. Everybody thinks it is in the tanks. The margin is in how many times you go, and how many times you go depends entirely on the queue, and the queue depends on 4 men, and 3 of the 4 men are reasonable.

Uncle A. has been on that road 16 years. He knows all 4. He does not pay more than the standard and he does not pay less, and he has never once been stopped for longer than an hour, and both of those facts are the same fact.
Now the part that is actually about me.
I am 17.

You cannot hold a licence for that route at 17. You cannot hold a lot of things at 17 and I have counted them: a licence, a bank account that does anything, a passport without my father, and a rented room in your own name.
So there is a name on the manifest and it is not mine.

It is a real man. He is 26 and he is my uncle's wife's cousin and he is in Tehran and he does not drive, and he gets a small amount every month for the use of it, and the arrangement is 4 years old and I inherited it from a boy who turned 21 and went to do something else.
I have driven 41 runs under that name.

I want to write down that this does not feel like anything. That is the honest answer. People think it must feel like something. It does not. You say a name at a barrier the way you say your own, and after about the 6th time it is your own, and the only moment it is strange is when somebody uses my actual name in a yard and it takes me half a second, and that half a second is the only part of any of this that ever frightens me.
Cost tonight: nothing, ate at my grandmother's.
The great-uncle sat against the wall and did not say anything for 40 minutes.
I counted. He said 11 words all evening and 4 of them were "yes."
Everyone thinks he is wonderful.
ACCOUNT 12
By the sixth week they had begun to plan around me and I did not notice until it had already happened, which is the whole of my defence and it is not one.
Here is what planning around a man looks like, and it is not dramatic and there is no moment.

In the third week Golbanu said, in a general way, that the room at the back had damp in it and something should be done before Esfand. In the fifth week her son Reza said he would look at the room at the back in Bahman, and Golbanu said, without any emphasis at all, that Bahman was too late.
In the sixth week the roll of insulation appeared in the yard.

Nobody said the words for him. Nobody has ever said the words for him. A roll of insulation arrived in a yard and leaned against a wall for eleven days and then a man came and did the room, and I was not consulted about any of it and would not have been, because you are not consulted about a house you live in.
And a woman at the bakery asked me — casually, as a piece of village business — whether I would still be here in Farvardin.
I said probably.

She said, "Good," and that was all, and by the following week two other people had asked me the same question in the same tone and I understood that they were not asking, they were confirming a thing they had already been told, and that somewhere in that house a sentence had been said about Farvardin that I had not been present for.
I want to put down what that does to a man in my position and I am going to be honest about it and it is not what you would expect.

It should have frightened me. Every previous coat had a clock on it and I could hear the clock from the first day — twelve days and a border, four days, four months until the pass opens, nine days of an inspection. The clock is the thing that makes it survivable.
This one has no clock.
And instead of that frightening me it did something much worse, which is that I began, quietly, without deciding to, to make plans of my own.

Small ones. I want to be precise about the scale of them because the scale is the point. I thought about the room at the back and whether the window would take a bar, which is a thing I have thought in every room I have ever been in, and then I thought about it a second time in a completely different way, which was whether it would take a curtain.
I have never in my adult life thought about a curtain.

That is the extent of it. The chair is still there. Nobody has moved it. I do not know which of the two of them it is for now and I do not think anybody in that house knows either, and I have decided that is the point of it.
There is a poem my grandmother tells wrong about birds who go looking for a king.
She only remembers the duck, who will not go because he lives in the water and is therefore always clean, and she thinks it is the funniest thing she has ever heard.
I asked her last week what happens to the duck.
She said nobody ever tells you that part.
I said somebody should find out.
And she said, "Well," and gave me more rice.

Aban [aa-BAAN] — The eighth month of the Iranian calendar, late
October to late November.

Benz — In Iranian usage, any of the long-serving Mercedes trucks that have carried the country's freight for half a century; the marque has become the noun.

Manteq al-Tayr [man-TEGH ot-TAYR] — Arabic, The Speech of the Birds, known in English as The Conference of the Birds. Attar's allegorical poem of c. 1177, in which the birds of the world set out across seven valleys to find their king, the Simorgh. Each bird first offers an excuse for not going. The nightingale is in love with a rose. The owl will not leave the ruins because there is treasure buried beneath them. The hawk already sits on a king's wrist, hooded and fed by hand. And the duck cannot leave the water, because he is always in it and therefore always clean, and cannot see why he should cross a desert and be dirtied. Their guide is the hoopoe. It is taught in
Iranian schools.
Nowruz [now-ROOZ] — Persian, new day. The Iranian new year, at the spring equinox; older than Islam, and the country's principal festival.
Sizdah [seez-DAH], the thirteenth day of it, spent outdoors.
Panjshanbeh [panj-shan-BEH] — Persian, Thursday, literally the fifth day. The eve of the Muslim holy day, and in Iran the night families gather — and the night families visit their dead.
qanat [gha-NAAT] — Arabic via Persian, channel. A hand-dug tunnel bringing water by gravity from an aquifer to a settlement.
Simorgh [see-MORGH] — Persian, from Middle Persian senmurw. The great bird of Persian myth; in the Shahnameh the protector of Zal, and in Attar the king the birds go to find.
